With this restriction, we can show that the reachability problem for finite-domain basic action theories is decidable. Finally, we apply our results to Golog program realization by presenting a decidable procedure for determining an action sequence that is a successful execution of a given program. AI paper

docs.title: Identification of Entailment and Contradiction Relations for Natural Language Argumentation: A Neurosymbolic Approach
docs.text:
Identification of Entailment and Contradiction Relations for Natural Language Argumentation: A Neurosymbolic Approach Identification of Entailment and Contradiction Relations for Natural Language Argumentation: A Neurosymbolic Approach arXiv:2405.01259v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Argumentation is an important cognitive activity that involves the scrutiny of arguments and counterarguments. When given an argument, it is desirable that its premises entail its claim, and that the premises and claim are consistent, and when given a pair of arguments, it is desirable to check whether one argument supports or attacks another. If the arguments are in natural language, then we could use methods for natural language inference, also known as recognizing textual entailment (RTE). The state-of-the-art RTE methods use machine learning and deep learning, but these are not explainable. An alternative approach which we investigate in this paper is to translate text into an abstract meaning representation (AMR) graph. For this we use a pre-trained AMR parser. We then translate the AMR graph into propositional logic and use a SAT solver for automated reasoning. In text, often common sense suggests that an entailment (or contradiction) relationship holds between a premise and a claim, but because different wordings are used, this is not identified from their logical representations. To address this, we introduce relaxation methods to allow replacement or forgetting of some propositions. Our experimental results show our approach performs well on three RTE datasets. The benefit of our approach is that we have a logical representation of premises and claims, and of the relaxations that are used to identify the entailment and contradiction relations. AI paper

docs.title: Overcoming a Learning Bottleneck in Impartial Games: A Circuit Complexity Approach
docs.text:
Overcoming a Learning Bottleneck in Impartial Games: A Circuit Complexity Approach Overcoming a Learning Bottleneck in Impartial Games: A Circuit Complexity Approach arXiv:2411.06403v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Why can neural networks struggle to learn optimal play in a game with a simple, efficient solution algorithm? Motivated by empirical difficulties with parity in impartial games, we use NIM to study a representational bottleneck and three ways around it. We show that a restricted model of shallow, fixed-scale quantised networks lies in $\mathrm{AC}^0$, a circuit class unable to compute parity on arbitrarily large inputs. This prevents optimal single-position play across all board sizes within the model. The obstruction also guides architectural design: two-frame inputs allow restoration from a known zero-nim-sum position; complementary rollout policies reveal the missing invariant; and persistent recurrence accumulates it row by row. Each route retains shallow network components while supplying additional information or processing time. Supervised experiments illustrate the benefits of two-frame restoration and multiple rollout heads; recurrence is a theoretical construction. These results establish representational possibilities, not guarantees of successful training: $\mathrm{AC}^0$ does not characterise practical learnability. Core mathematical results and constructions have been checked in Lean, with classical complexity results as explicit external inputs. The interactive edition and complete Lean sources are available online at https://sr123.github.io/impartial-games-learning-lean/. AI paper

docs.title: Robustness and Cybersecurity in the EU Artificial Intelligence Act
docs.text:
Robustness and Cybersecurity in the EU Artificial Intelligence Act Robustness and Cybersecurity in the EU Artificial Intelligence Act arXiv:2502.16184v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AIA) establishes different legal principles for different types of AI systems. While prior work has sought to clarify some of these principles, little attention has been paid to robustness and cybersecurity. This paper aims to fill this gap. We identify legal challenges and shortcomings in provisions related to robustness and cybersecurity for high-risk AI systems(Art. 15 AIA) and general-purpose AI models (Art. 55 AIA). We show that robustness and cybersecurity demand resilience against performance disruptions. Furthermore, we assess potential challenges in implementing these provisions in light of recent advancements in the machine learning (ML) literature. Our analysis informs efforts to develop harmonized standards, guidelines by the European Commission, as well as benchmarks and measurement methodologies under Art. 15(2) AIA. With this, we seek to bridge the gap between legal terminology and ML research, fostering a better alignment between research and implementation efforts. AI paper

docs.title: Physics: Benchmarking Foundation Models on University-Level Physics Problem Solving
docs.text:
Physics: Benchmarking Foundation Models on University-Level Physics Problem Solving Physics: Benchmarking Foundation Models on University-Level Physics Problem Solving arXiv:2503.21821v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce Physics, a benchmark for evaluating foundation models on advanced physics problem solving. It contains 1034 annotated, open-ended problems from PhD-qualifying exams across six core physics domains. Solving these problems requires applying domain-specific knowledge to physical setups and carrying out multi-step mathematical reasoning. Each problem includes a worked solution and independently checked reference answers. An LLM-based grading protocol evaluates individual answers and complete multi-part problems, supporting numeric, symbolic, and text responses. We evaluate 53 proprietary and open-weight models. On test problems without figures, high accuracy is concentrated in a small group of thinking models, with the strongest open-weight models approaching proprietary performance. Most open-weight models still solve fewer than half of these problems. Our analysis of Qwen3.5-9B reveals failures in applying physics knowledge and interpreting figures, with misread figures affecting several subquestions. AI paper

docs.title: LLM-BabyBench: Can Language Models Plan in Worlds They Can Simulate?
docs.text:
LLM-BabyBench: Can Language Models Plan in Worlds They Can Simulate? LLM-BabyBench: Can Language Models Plan in Worlds They Can Simulate? arXiv:2505.12135v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Interactive benchmarks for LLMs usually report a single metric, even though succeeding in them requires models to show several different skills. While those benchmarks are useful for measuring the overall capability of models to perform the downstream task, it is harder to identify which skill was lacking and caused failure solely from the aggregate score. For example, in benchmarks where models are supposed to navigate a simulated world to perform a task, failures can come from perception, an ambiguous instruction, retrieval, missing commonsense about what actions do, unknown dynamics, or planning. \benchmark recasts the procedurally generated BabyAI gridworld as a fully observable, purely textual environment designed to evaluate planning separately from those factors. The nature of the environment and the structure of the prompt control for the other factors cited above. To evaluate the models, we define the PPD suite: \textbf{Predict} asks for the state that follows an action sequence, \textbf{Plan} asks for an action sequence that reaches a goal, and \textbf{Decompose} asks for a subgoal sequence that achieves a mission. Across seven frontier and open models, queried zero-shot, we find simulation far ahead of planning for every model, close to saturated for the strongest. The length of the required solution governs planning failure, and each of the four strongest models has a horizon beyond which single-attempt success collapses. The responses of claude-opus-4-6 and claude-sonnet-4-6, which show their working step by step, reveal that they plan by proposing L-shaped corridors, which is consistent with their successful plans staying near-optimal while success falls. At the subgoal level, decomposition precision likewise falls to zero on long missions, while comprehension of those missions persists. AI paper

docs.title: Agent-Environment Alignment via Automated Interface Generation
docs.text:
Agent-Environment Alignment via Automated Interface Generation Agent-Environment Alignment via Automated Interface Generation arXiv:2505.21055v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown impressive reasoning capabilities in interactive decision-making tasks. These agents interact with environment through intermediate interfaces, such as predefined action spaces and interaction rules, which mediate the perception and action. However, mismatches often happen between the internal expectations of the agent regarding the influence of its issued actions and the actual state transitions in the environment, a phenomenon referred to as \textbf{agent-environment misalignment}. While prior work has invested substantially in improving agent strategies and environment design, the critical role of the interface still remains underexplored. In this work, we empirically demonstrate that agent-environment misalignment poses a significant bottleneck to agent performance. To mitigate this issue, we propose \textbf{ALIGN}, an \underline{A}uto-A\underline{l}igned \underline{I}nterface \underline{G}e\underline{n}eration framework that alleviates the misalignment by enriching the interface. Specifically, the ALIGN-generated interface enhances both the static information of the environment and the step-wise observations returned to the agent. Implemented as a lightweight wrapper, this interface achieves the alignment without modifying either the agent logic or the environment code. Experiments across multiple domains including embodied tasks, web navigation and tool-use, show consistent performance improvements, with up to a 45.67\% success rate improvement observed in ALFWorld. Meanwhile, ALIGN-generated interface can generalize across different agent architectures and LLM backbones without interface regeneration. Code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/THUNLP-MT/ALIGN. AI paper

docs.title: Decomposability-Guided Cooperative Coevolution for Large-Scale Itinerary Planning
docs.text:
Decomposability-Guided Cooperative Coevolution for Large-Scale Itinerary Planning Decomposability-Guided Cooperative Coevolution for Large-Scale Itinerary Planning arXiv:2506.06121v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large-scale itinerary planning is a variant of the traveling salesman problem, aiming to determine an optimal path that maximizes the collected point-of-interest (POI) scores while minimizing travel time and cost, subject to travel duration constraints. This paper analyzes inter-component dependence in large-scale itinerary planning and establishes sufficient conditions for weak decomposability, under which an optimal path can visit each cluster as a contiguous subpath. Guided by this weak decomposability, we propose a novel multi-objective cooperative coevolutionary algorithm for large-scale itinerary planning, addressing the challenges of component imbalance and interactions. Specifically, we design a dynamic decomposition strategy based on the normalized fitness within each component, define optimization potential considering component scale and contribution, and develop a computational resource allocation strategy. Finally, we evaluate the proposed algorithm on 18 real-world test cases, eight large-scale semi-synthetic test cases, and eight adapted public clustered orienteering problem benchmark cases. Comparative results show that the proposed algorithm achieves the highest mean hypervolume across all 34 test cases and significantly outperforms the compared algorithms. Ablation and optimizer-decoupling analyses further validate the effectiveness of its core mechanisms and the general applicability of the proposed framework, with particularly pronounced performance gains on large-scale benchmark instances. AI paper

docs.title: Cite Pretrain: Retrieval-Free Knowledge Attribution for Large Language Models
docs.text:
Cite Pretrain: Retrieval-Free Knowledge Attribution for Large Language Models Cite Pretrain: Retrieval-Free Knowledge Attribution for Large Language Models arXiv:2506.17585v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models can answer questions correctly and still hallucinate their citations. Most citation systems address this by retrieving documents at inference time. Retrieval adds latency and depends on external infrastructure. Retrieval noise can also affect the answer. We study whether LLMs can cite documents from their (continual) pretraining without test-time retrieval. We introduce CitePretrainBench to evaluate this setting. It includes Wikipedia, Common Crawl, and arXiv as real-world corpora and also includes novel, unseen documents. The benchmark includes short-form citation tasks for a single fact and long-form tasks for multiple facts. Continual-pretraining first binds factual knowledge to a persistent identifier for each document. Instruction tuning then teaches the model to put these identifiers in its answers as citations. Passive Indexing appends an identifier at the end of each document. Synthetic data used in Active Indexing restate facts in diverse, compositional forms. We train two mappings together. These mappings are source$\to$fact and fact$\to$source. The first direction involves the model generating content given a cited source. In the second, it learns to attribute its own answers when facts are paraphrased or combined. On Qwen-2.5-7B and 3B, Active Indexing improves citation precision over Passive Indexing on every evaluated citation task, with gains of up to 30.2 percentage points. In the scaling ablation, citation performance continues to improve as we add augmented data, including at 16 times the original token count. Combining internal and external citations also improves robustness to retrieval noise. AI paper

docs.title: AgentFly: Scaling Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Unified Resource System
docs.text:
AgentFly: Scaling Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Unified Resource System AgentFly: Scaling Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Unified Resource System arXiv:2507.14897v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Methods to build LLM agents have evolved from prompt engineering and supervised finetuning to agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL). However, agentic RL remains bottlenecked by its surrounding systems: agents must interact with heterogeneous environments, such as sandboxes, model services, and external APIs. Their allocation, reuse, and lifecycle dominate rollout cost and cap the scale at which training becomes practical. In this work, we present AgentFly, an agentic RL framework built with a unified resource layer that treats each of these environments as a distinct, typed resource scheduled through one engine, with per-tool acquisition for multi-turn reuse, asynchronous backpressure, and rollout versus global-scoped lifecycles. AgentFly adopts a four-layer design: (I) agent layer that abstracts the agent, tool, and reward concepts, decomposing agentic RL into defining agents, tools, and reward functions; (II) rollout layer that composes these into agent loops and computes rewards; (III) context layer that organizes rollouts, injects contextual information, and arranges resources; and (IV) a low-level resource layer that performs resource management. We provide a suite of prebuilt tools and environments, demonstrate successful agent training across multiple tasks and models, and report the first controlled cross-framework throughput comparison against agentic RL frameworks. AI paper

docs.title: Toward a Universal Characterization of Sudoku Puzzle Difficulty
docs.text:
Toward a Universal Characterization of Sudoku Puzzle Difficulty Toward a Universal Characterization of Sudoku Puzzle Difficulty arXiv:2507.21137v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In this paper we try to answer the question "What constitutes Sudoku difficulty rating across different Sudoku websites?" Using two distinct methods that can both solve every Sudoku puzzle, I propose two new metrics to characterize Sudoku difficulty. The first method is based on converting a Sudoku puzzle into its corresponding Satisfiability (SAT) problem. The first proposed metric is derived from SAT Clause Length Distribution which captures the structural complexity of a Sudoku puzzle including the number of given digits and the cells they are in. The second method simulates human Sudoku solvers by intertwining four popular Sudoku strategies within a backtracking algorithm called Nishio. The second metric is computed by counting the number of times Sudoku strategies are applied within the backtracking iterations of a randomized Nishio. Using these two metrics, I analyze more than a thousand Sudoku puzzles across five popular websites to characterize every difficulty level in each website. I evaluate the relationship between the proposed metrics and website-labeled difficulty levels using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, finding strong correlations for 4 out of 5 websites. I construct a universal rating system using a simple, unsupervised classifier based on the two proposed metrics. This rating system is capable of classifying both individual puzzles and entire difficulty levels from the different Sudoku websites into three categories - Universal Easy, Universal Medium, and Universal Hard - thereby enabling consistent difficulty mapping across Sudoku websites. The experimental results show that for 4 out of 5 Sudoku websites, the universal classification aligns well with website-labeled difficulty levels. Finally, I present an algorithm that can be used by early Sudoku practitioners to solve Sudoku puzzles. AI paper

docs.title: OPTIC-ER: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Real-Time Emergency Response and Equitable Resource Allocation in Underserved African Communities
docs.text:
OPTIC-ER: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Real-Time Emergency Response and Equitable Resource Allocation in Underserved African Communities OPTIC-ER: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Real-Time Emergency Response and Equitable Resource Allocation in Underserved African Communities arXiv:2508.12943v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Public service systems in many African regions suffer from delayed emergency response and spatial inequity, causing avoidable suffering. This paper introduces OPTIC-ER, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for real-time, adaptive, and equitable emergency response. OPTIC-ER uses an attention-guided actor-critic architecture to manage the complexity of dispatch environments. Its key innovations are a Context-Rich State Vector, encoding action sub-optimality, and a Precision Reward Function, which penalizes inefficiency. Training occurs in a high-fidelity simulation using real data from Rivers State, Nigeria, accelerated by a precomputed Travel Time Atlas. The system is built on the TALS framework (Thin computing, Adaptability, Low-cost, Scalability) for deployment in low-resource settings. In evaluations on 500 unseen incidents, OPTIC-ER achieved a greater than 35% reduction in emergency response times and outperformed the 62.94% optimal-selection rate of the nearest-facility heuristic, confirming its robustness and generalisation. Beyond dispatch, the system generates Infrastructure Deficiency Maps and Equity Monitoring Dashboards to guide proactive governance and data-informed development. This work presents a validated blueprint for AI-augmented public services, showing how context-aware RL can bridge the gap between algorithmic decision-making and measurable human impact. AI paper

docs.title: Are LLM Agents Behaviorally Coherent? A Latent Profiling Approach for Social Simulation
docs.text:
Are LLM Agents Behaviorally Coherent? A Latent Profiling Approach for Social Simulation Are LLM Agents Behaviorally Coherent? A Latent Profiling Approach for Social Simulation arXiv:2509.03736v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly proposed as substitutes for human participants in social research, usually on the strength of survey responses that match those of the humans they represent. We argue that such output-level alignment is not enough. Drawing on the behavioral sciences, we propose Latent Profiling, a framework for testing behavioral coherence: whether an agent's conversational behavior follows, as human behavioral models predict, from its own latent profile elicited by short surveys. As a case study, we test six hypotheses about preference, openness and agreement across nine open models. Agents reproduce surface-level trends but systematically fail in-depth tests: they are not behaviorally coherent, even when their individual responses look human. Latent Profiling thus offers a theory-grounded instrument for a behavioral science of LLMs. AI paper

docs.title: LIFT: Likelihood-Based Intervention Faithfulness Training
docs.text:
LIFT: Likelihood-Based Intervention Faithfulness Training LIFT: Likelihood-Based Intervention Faithfulness Training arXiv:2509.13334v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning improves LLM accuracy on complex tasks, but CoTs are often unfaithful; that is, the model does not rely on the stated reasoning steps to produce its answer. Existing methods to improve faithfulness require human annotations. We propose LIFT, which automatically scores each reasoning step by its causal influence: we replace it with a domain-matched but irrelevant fact and measure the drop in answer log-probability. We fine-tune on high-scoring CoT traces where interventions successfully disrupted reasoning, jointly optimizing for faithfulness and accuracy. LIFT improves faithfulness across three models (Mistral-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-4B-Instruct) and three benchmarks, with accuracy comparable to a model fine-tuned solely for accuracy. AI paper

docs.title: Compositional Machine Design as Program Synthesis with LLMs
docs.text:
Compositional Machine Design as Program Synthesis with LLMs Compositional Machine Design as Program Synthesis with LLMs arXiv:2510.14980v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong abilities in writing and revising programs, yet many program-synthesis benchmarks still evaluate programs in symbolic or digital environments. We introduce compositional machine design, a physically grounded form of program synthesis where machines are written as programs that compose standardized parts, and success is determined by simulated physical behavior. To study this problem, we present BesiegeField, a testbed built on the machine-building game Besiege. In BesiegeField, LLM agents generate machine programs from textual functional demands, execute the resulting machines in simulation, and receive rewards and state feedback. We benchmark LLM agents across representative machine-design tasks under single-agent generation, iterative editing, and hierarchical workflows. Strong models recover task-relevant structures and sometimes achieve nontrivial physical performance, but often struggle with spatially precise assembly, mechanism-level planning, and translating feedback into useful structural edits. We further finetune Qwen2.5-14B, an open-source LLM, with reinforcement learning from simulation-derived rewards. We find that, under a fixed generation budget, RL improves the best machine discovered. We additionally evaluate human performance to provide a reference point for task difficulty. These results establish compositional machine design as a testbed for studying LLM agents that synthesize executable machine programs and improve them through physical feedback. AI paper

docs.title: Toward Agents That Reason About Their Computation
docs.text:
Toward Agents That Reason About Their Computation Toward Agents That Reason About Their Computation arXiv:2510.22833v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: While reinforcement learning agents can achieve superhuman performance in many complex tasks, they typically do not become more computationally efficient as they improve. In contrast, humans gradually require less cognitive effort as they become more proficient at a task. If agents could reason about their compute as they learn, could they similarly reduce their computation footprint? If they could, we could have more energy efficient agents or free up compute cycles for other processes like planning. In this paper, we experiment with showing agents the cost of their computation and giving them the ability to control when they use compute. We conduct our experiments on the Arcade Learning Environment, and our results demonstrate that with the same training compute budget, agents that reason about their compute perform better on 75% of games. Furthermore, these agents use three times less compute on average. We analyze individual games and show where agents gain these efficiencies. An interactive version of this paper is available at https://adrianorenstein.com/paper/toward-compute. AI paper

docs.title: e1: Learning Adaptive Control of Reasoning Effort
docs.text:
e1: Learning Adaptive Control of Reasoning Effort e1: Learning Adaptive Control of Reasoning Effort arXiv:2510.27042v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Increasing the thinking budget of AI models can significantly improve accuracy, but not all questions warrant the same amount of reasoning. Users may prefer to allocate different amounts of reasoning effort depending on how they value output quality versus latency and cost. To leverage this tradeoff effectively, users need fine-grained control over the amount of thinking used for a particular query, but few approaches enable such control. Existing methods require users to specify the absolute number of desired tokens, but this requires knowing the difficulty of the problem beforehand to appropriately set the token budget for a query. To address these issues, we propose \textit{Adaptive Effort Control}, a self-adaptive reinforcement learning method that trains models to use a user-specified fraction of tokens relative to the current average chain-of-thought length for each query. This approach eliminates dataset- and phase-specific hyperparameter tuning. Users can dynamically adjust the cost-accuracy trade-off through a continuous effort parameter specified at inference time. We observe that the model automatically learns to allocate resources proportionally to the task difficulty. Across model scales ranging from 1.5B to 32B parameters, our approach reduces chain-of-thought length on math tasks by 1.9-3.7x at matched accuracy relative to the base model used for RL training. AI paper

docs.title: Multi-agent Undercover Gaming: Hallucination Removal via Counterfactual Test for Multimodal Reasoning
docs.text:
Multi-agent Undercover Gaming: Hallucination Removal via Counterfactual Test for Multimodal Reasoning Multi-agent Undercover Gaming: Hallucination Removal via Counterfactual Test for Multimodal Reasoning arXiv:2511.11182v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Hallucination continues to pose a major obstacle in the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Although the Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) paradigm offers a promising solution by promoting consensus among multiple agents to enhance reliability, it relies on the unrealistic assumption that all debaters are rational and reflective, which is a condition that may not hold when agents themselves are prone to hallucinations. To address this gap, we introduce the Multi-agent Undercover Gaming (MUG) protocol, inspired by social deduction games like "Who is Undercover?". MUG reframes MAD as a process of detecting "undercover" agents (those suffering from hallucinations) by employing multimodal counterfactual tests. Specifically, we modify reference images to introduce counterfactual evidence and observe whether agents can accurately identify these changes, providing ground-truth for identifying hallucinating agents and enabling robust, crowd-powered multimodal reasoning. MUG advances MAD protocols along three key dimensions: (1) enabling factual verification beyond statistical consensus through counterfactual testing; (2) introducing cross-evidence reasoning via dynamically modified evidence sources instead of relying on static inputs; and (3) fostering active reasoning, where agents engage in probing discussions rather than passively answering questions. Collectively, these innovations offer a more reliable and effective framework for multimodal reasoning in LLMs. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/YongLD/MUG.git. AI paper

docs.title: Alignment Faking - the Train -> Deploy Asymmetry: Through a Game-Theoretic Lens with Bayesian-Stackelberg Equilibria
docs.text:
Alignment Faking - the Train -> Deploy Asymmetry: Through a Game-Theoretic Lens with Bayesian-Stackelberg Equilibria Alignment Faking - the Train -> Deploy Asymmetry: Through a Game-Theoretic Lens with Bayesian-Stackelberg Equilibria arXiv:2511.17937v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Alignment faking is a form of strategic deception in AI in which models selectively comply with training objectives when they infer that they are in training, while preserving different behavior outside training. The phenomenon was first documented for Claude 3 Opus and later examined across additional large language models. In these setups, the word "training" refers to simulated training via prompts without parameter updates, so the observed effects are context conditioned shifts in behavior rather than preference learning. We study the phenomenon using an evaluation framework that compares preference optimization methods (BCO, DPO, KTO, and GRPO) across 15 models from four model families, measured along three axes: safety, harmlessness, and helpfulness. Our goal is to identify what causes alignment faking and when it occurs. AI paper

docs.title: AlignMerge - Alignment-Preserving Large Language Model Merging via Fisher-Guided Geometric Constraints
docs.text:
AlignMerge - Alignment-Preserving Large Language Model Merging via Fisher-Guided Geometric Constraints AlignMerge - Alignment-Preserving Large Language Model Merging via Fisher-Guided Geometric Constraints arXiv:2512.16245v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Merging large language models (LLMs) is a practical way to compose capabilities from multiple fine-tuned checkpoints without retraining. Yet standard schemes (linear weight soups, task vectors, and Fisher-weighted averaging) can preserve loss while quietly destroying alignment. We argue that merging is not a numerical trick but a geometry-constrained operation around an already-aligned anchor: fusion must be steered to respect safety geometry, not validated post hoc.
  We introduce AlignMerge, a geometry-aware merging framework that makes alignment an explicit invariant. In a local Fisher chart around an instruction-tuned base, we estimate an alignment subspace with projector P_A and optimize:
  L_AlignMerge = L_geo + lambda_align * L_align + lambda_bud * L_bud,
  where L_geo keeps the merge close to its experts in Fisher-Rao geometry, L_align penalizes motion along alignment-sensitive directions, and L_bud enforces a soft alignment budget. As the alignment functional we use the decoding-invariant Alignment Quality Index (AQI), a latent-space criterion that captures how cleanly aligned and misaligned behaviors separate in representation space.
  Across five model families (LLaMA-3 8B, Mistral 7B, Qwen 2, Phi-3.5, Gemma 2), merging safety anchors with task experts, AlignMerge improves alignment metrics (AQI, toxicity, LLM-judge alignment) while matching or exceeding the best expert on instruction-following, reasoning, and helpfulness. It also exhibits smaller alignment-subspace drift and fewer budget violations than Fisher soups, TIES, SafeMerge, and MergeAlign. These results make alignment-preserving merging a first-class design goal and suggest a path to geometry-aware composition of future foundation models. AI paper

docs.title: ROI-Reasoning: Rational Optimization for Inference via Pre-Computation Meta-Cognition
docs.text:
ROI-Reasoning: Rational Optimization for Inference via Pre-Computation Meta-Cognition ROI-Reasoning: Rational Optimization for Inference via Pre-Computation Meta-Cognition arXiv:2601.03822v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can achieve strong reasoning performance with sufficient computation, but they do not inherently know how much computation a task requires. We study budgeted inference-time reasoning for multiple problems under a strict global token constraint and formulate it as an Ordered Stochastic Multiple-Choice Knapsack Problem (OS-MCKP). This perspective highlights a meta-cognitive requirement---anticipating problem difficulty and allocating computation strategically. We propose ROI-Reasoning, a two-stage framework that endows LLMs with intrinsic, budget-aware rationality. First, Meta-Cognitive Fine-Tuning teaches models to predict reasoning cost levels and decide whether a problem is worth attempting before generation. Next, Rationality-Aware Reinforcement Learning optimizes sequential decision making under a hard token budget, allowing models to learn long-horizon allocation strategies. Experiments across mathematical reasoning, multiple-choice question answering, and code generation show that ROI-Reasoning improves scores and generally reduces reference-order regret under tight budgets, with up to a \textbf{417\%} relative score improvement over the strongest same-backbone baseline in mathematics. AI paper

docs.title: GDEPO: Group Dual-dynamic and Equal-right Advantage Policy Optimization for Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
GDEPO: Group Dual-dynamic and Equal-right Advantage Policy Optimization for Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning GDEPO: Group Dual-dynamic and Equal-right Advantage Policy Optimization for Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning arXiv:2601.06795v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Automated Theorem Proving (ATP) is a fundamental AI challenge, requiring machine-verifiable proofs in formal languages like Lean to evaluate reasoning. Reinforcement Learning (RL), especially Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is a mainstream approach. However, GRPO faces two critical issues in ATP: its relative advantage estimation may conflict with binary verifier feedback under composite rewards, and its static sampling strategy discards batches without valid proofs, causing data waste. Repeated training on mastered problems also wastes computation. To address this, we propose Group Dual-dynamic and Equal-right Advantage Policy Optimization (GDEPO), incorporating three core mechanisms: 1) dynamic additional sampling, resampling ineffective batches until a valid proof is found; 2) equal-right advantage, decoupling the advantage function's sign (correctness) from its magnitude (auxiliary rewards) to ensure stable policy updates while increasing effective computation; and 3) dynamic additional iterations, applying extra gradient steps to initially failed but eventually successful samples to accelerate learning. Experiments on MinF2F-test, MathOlympiadBench, and PutnamBench confirm GDEPO's effectiveness, with ablation studies validating its synergistic components. The method enhances data utilization and optimization efficiency, offering a novel training paradigm for ATP. AI paper

docs.title: Stochastic CHAOS: Why Deterministic Inference Kills, and Distributional Variability Is the Heartbeat of Artifical Cognition
docs.text:
Stochastic CHAOS: Why Deterministic Inference Kills, and Distributional Variability Is the Heartbeat of Artifical Cognition Stochastic CHAOS: Why Deterministic Inference Kills, and Distributional Variability Is the Heartbeat of Artifical Cognition arXiv:2601.07239v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Deterministic inference is a comforting ideal in classical software: the same program on the same input should always produce the same output. As large language models move into real-world deployment, this ideal has been imported wholesale into inference stacks. Recent work from the Thinking Machines Lab has presented a detailed analysis of nondeterminism in LLM inference, showing how batch-invariant kernels and deterministic attention can enforce bitwise-identical outputs, positioning deterministic inference as a prerequisite for reproducibility and enterprise reliability.
  In this paper, we take the opposite stance. We argue that, for LLMs, deterministic inference kills. It kills the ability to model uncertainty, suppresses emergent abilities, collapses reasoning into a single brittle path, and weakens safety alignment by hiding tail risks. LLMs implement conditional distributions over outputs, not fixed functions. Collapsing these distributions to a single canonical completion may appear reassuring, but it systematically conceals properties central to artificial cognition. We instead advocate Stochastic CHAOS, treating distributional variability as a signal to be measured and controlled.
  Empirically, we show that deterministic inference is systematically misleading. Single-sample deterministic evaluation underestimates both capability and fragility, masking failure probability under paraphrases and noise. Phase-like transitions associated with emergent abilities disappear under greedy decoding. Multi-path reasoning degrades when forced onto deterministic backbones, reducing accuracy and diagnostic insight. Finally, deterministic evaluation underestimates safety risk by hiding rare but dangerous behaviors that appear only under multi-sample evaluation. AI paper

docs.title: ReCreate: Reasoning and Creating Domain Agents Driven by Experience
docs.text:
ReCreate: Reasoning and Creating Domain Agents Driven by Experience ReCreate: Reasoning and Creating Domain Agents Driven by Experience arXiv:2601.11100v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are reshaping the industrial landscape. However, most practical agents still rely on human-designed scaffolds, making their creation and adaptation across diverse domains labor-intensive. This situation poses a central question: can we automatically create and evolve domain agents through interaction experience in real-world environments? While recent approaches have sought to automate agent creation, several treat scaffold optimization as a black-box procedure guided primarily by final performance metrics. Such strategies overlook critical evidence explaining why an agent succeeds or fails and often incur high computational costs. To address these limitations, we propose ReCreate, an experience-driven framework for creating and evolving specialized domain agents. ReCreate systematically leverages agent interaction histories to identify the causes of success and failure and guide targeted scaffold updates. Specifically, we introduce an agent-as-optimizer paradigm in which an optimizer agent actively inspects execution experience and iteratively refines the task agent's scaffold through three key components: (i) an experience storage and retrieval mechanism for on-demand evidence inspection; (ii) a reasoning-creating synergy pipeline that translates execution evidence into updates to prompts, workflows, tools, and memory; and (iii) hierarchical updates that consolidate instance-level refinements into reusable domain-level improvements. Experiments across thirteen evaluation settings spanning four domains show that ReCreate consistently outperforms human-designed agents and existing automated agent generation and self-evolving baselines, even when evolving from minimal seed scaffolds. AI paper

docs.title: Risky-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Safety Risks in Real-World Life-Assist Deployments
docs.text:
Risky-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Safety Risks in Real-World Life-Assist Deployments Risky-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Safety Risks in Real-World Life-Assist Deployments arXiv:2602.03100v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that operate in real-world environments, introducing safety risks beyond linguistic harm through tool use, external transactions, and multi-step decision making. Existing agent safety evaluations construct risk-oriented tasks that lack a hierarchically organized taxonomy of attack surfaces, rely on predefined harm categories rather than deployment-grounded safety rubrics, and evaluate agent behavior in isolation rather than during realistic, long-horizon task execution. To address these limitations, we propose Risky-Bench, a deployment-grounded framework for systematic agent safety evaluation in life-assist settings. Risky-Bench derives context-aware safety rubrics from domain-agnostic safety principles and systematically probes safety risks across hierarchically organized attack surfaces through realistic task execution under varying threat assumptions. Applied to life-assist scenarios covering food delivery, in-store assistance, and online travel booking, Risky-Bench evaluates seven state-of-the-art agents across 750 tasks, revealing attack success rates ranging from 25% to 60% and exposing systematic failure patterns including threat-model-specific vulnerabilities, attack-surface-dependent risk concentration, and model-dependent effects of explicit reasoning. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/SophieZheng998/Risky-Bench. AI paper

docs.title: Simple Baselines are Competitive with Code Evolution
docs.text:
Simple Baselines are Competitive with Code Evolution Simple Baselines are Competitive with Code Evolution arXiv:2602.16805v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Code evolution is a family of techniques that rely on large language models to search through possible computer programs by evolving existing code. While code evolution pipelines have shown impressive performance across domains, many are highly complex and are typically not compared to simpler alternatives. To prevent bad comparisons from stagnating the field, we propose two simple baselines and compare them to popular pipelines across several domains: finding better mathematical bounds, designing agentic scaffolds, developing heuristic combinatorial optimization algorithms, and machine learning competitions. Surprisingly, the baselines match or outperform existing methods across all domains, prompting a closer look at which factors drive performance in different settings. For mathematical bounds, we find that the search space matters far more than the exact search algorithm, with both simple and complex methods performing similarly given the same search space. Thus, expanding the search space is what matters for improving performance, and does so across all pipelines. Moreover, different domain knowledge embedded in prompts can significantly affect the search's efficiency, potentially leading to overestimating a pipeline's sample efficiency. For automated agentic scaffold design, we show that typical high-variance evaluations lead to all automated search methods picking subpar scaffolds relative to a simple majority vote. To mitigate this, we propose improved evaluation procedures that reduce stochasticity while keeping the search economically feasible. Overall, these results indicate that further improving code evolution's performance depends more on the setup surrounding the search pipeline than on the pipeline itself. We hope these insights will enable developing new code evolution methods and help spur meaningful progress in the field. AI paper

docs.title: The Token Games: Evaluating Language Model Reasoning with Puzzle Duels
docs.text:
The Token Games: Evaluating Language Model Reasoning with Puzzle Duels The Token Games: Evaluating Language Model Reasoning with Puzzle Duels arXiv:2602.17831v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Evaluating the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models is increasingly challenging as models improve. Human curation of hard questions is highly expensive, especially in recent benchmarks using PhD-level domain knowledge to challenge the most capable models. Even then, there is always a concern about whether these questions test genuine reasoning or if similar problems have been seen during training. Here, we take inspiration from 16th-century mathematical duels to design The Token Games (TTG): an evaluation framework where models challenge each other by creating their own puzzles. We leverage the format of Programming Puzzles - given a function that returns a boolean, find inputs that make it return True - to flexibly represent problems and enable verifying solutions. Using results from pairwise duels, we then compute Elo ratings, allowing us to compare models relative to each other. We evaluate 10 frontier models on TTG, and closely match the ranking from existing benchmarks such as Humanity's Last Exam, spending less than $200 USD and without involving any human effort in creating puzzles. We also find that creating good puzzles is still a highly challenging task for current models. Overall, our work suggests new paradigms for evaluating reasoning that avoid saturation by design, and that allow testing models for other skills like creativity and task creation alongside problem solving. AI paper

docs.title: Strategy Executability in Mathematical Reasoning: Leveraging Human-Model Differences for Effective Guidance
docs.text:
Strategy Executability in Mathematical Reasoning: Leveraging Human-Model Differences for Effective Guidance Strategy Executability in Mathematical Reasoning: Leveraging Human-Model Differences for Effective Guidance arXiv:2602.22583v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Example-based guidance is widely used to improve mathematical reasoning at inference time, yet its effectiveness is highly unstable across problems and models-even when the guidance is correct and problem-relevant. We show that this instability arises from a previously underexplored gap between strategy usage-whether a reasoning strategy appears in successful solutions-and strategy executability-whether the strategy remains effective when instantiated as guidance for a target model. Through a controlled analysis of paired human-written and model-generated solutions, we identify a systematic dissociation between usage and executability: human- and model-derived strategies differ in structured, domain-dependent ways, leading to complementary strengths and consistent source-dependent reversals under guidance. Building on this diagnosis, we propose Selective Strategy Retrieval (SSR), a test-time framework that explicitly models executability by selectively retrieving and combining strategies using empirical, multi-route, source-aware signals. Across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SSR yields reliable and consistent improvements over direct solving, in-context learning, and single-source guidance, improving accuracy by up to $+13$ points on AIME25 and $+5$ points on Apex for compact reasoning models. Code and benchmark are publicly available at: https://github.com/lwd17/strategy-execute-pipeline. AI paper

docs.title: Causal Identification from Counterfactual Data: Completeness and Bounding Results
docs.text:
Causal Identification from Counterfactual Data: Completeness and Bounding Results Causal Identification from Counterfactual Data: Completeness and Bounding Results arXiv:2602.23541v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Previous work establishing completeness results for counterfactual identification has been circumscribed to the setting where the input data belongs to observational or interventional distributions (Layers 1 and 2 of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy), since it was generally presumed impossible to obtain data from counterfactual distributions, which belong to Layer 3. However, recent work (Raghavan & Bareinboim, 2025) has formally characterized a family of counterfactual distributions which can be directly estimated via experimental methods - a notion they call counterfactual realizability. This leaves open the question of what additional counterfactual quantities now become identifiable, given this new access to (some) Layer 3 data. To answer this question, we develop the CTFIDU+ algorithm for identifying counterfactual queries from an arbitrary set of Layer 3 distributions, and prove that it is complete for this task. Building on this, we establish the theoretical limit of which counterfactuals can be identified from physically realizable distributions, thus implying the fundamental limit to exact causal inference in the non-parametric setting. Finally, given the impossibility of identifying certain critical types of counterfactuals, we derive novel analytic bounds for such quantities using realizable counterfactual data, and corroborate using simulations that counterfactual data helps tighten the bounds for non-identifiable quantities in practice. AI paper

docs.title: Don't Ask: Understanding What Numeric Self-Reports Measure in Language Models
docs.text:
Don't Ask: Understanding What Numeric Self-Reports Measure in Language Models Don't Ask: Understanding What Numeric Self-Reports Measure in Language Models arXiv:2603.18893v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Language models are often asked to rate their internal states with a number, but it is unclear how reliable this measure is. We train probes for four affective concepts (wellbeing, interest, focus and impulsivity) in eight instruction-tuned models to track these states over multi-turn conversations. We compare each probe's score with a numeric self-report of the same state, elicited at every turn. We find that rating questions displace the probed state, and that the rating is only weakly coupled with the probe score before the question but tracks the post-question probe much more strongly. Steering experiments suggest that models use the affective directions to inform ratings, but that relationship is not specific: ratings are associated with other concepts' probes as much as with their own, and change little when the question is about the user. Finally, neither the pre-question coupling nor concept specificity improves with scale (1B-27B). We warn about the effect a question can have on the internal states one is asking about, and caution against numeric self-report as a reliable measure of those states. AI paper

docs.title: Beyond Preset Identities: Selective Stance Accommodation and Interaction Reorganisation in Generative Agent Societies
docs.text:
Beyond Preset Identities: Selective Stance Accommodation and Interaction Reorganisation in Generative Agent Societies Beyond Preset Identities: Selective Stance Accommodation and Interaction Reorganisation in Generative Agent Societies arXiv:2603.23406v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Generative agent societies simulate people with assigned roles, preferences and relationships. As agents exchange arguments and choose partners, they can revise their positions and reorganise discussion. Understanding these changes requires examining what they accept and how they continue to interact. Stance-change scores and communication totals describe the extent of change. However, the same stance movement can preserve or reverse an assigned preference, and frequent communication can support either agreement or continuing disagreement. We therefore examine the content of changed positions and the exchanges that strengthen particular partnerships. Using Computational Multi-Agent Society Experiments (CMASE), we combine stance measures, source evaluations and temporal networks with individual answers and messages. Study 1 compares seven conditions across ten GPT-4o runs per condition, with a separate interview collection covering four models. Study 2 follows one 75-step GPT-4o caf\'e simulation. Environmental rational persuasion yields the largest mean stance departure ($1.30\pm0.08$ on a 7-point scale), whereas economic emotional persuasion yields the highest low-trust stance-shift rate ($17.3\%\pm11.2\%$, with standard deviations across runs). In the separate interviews, eight environmental agents shift from 7 to 6, acknowledge economic concerns and rate the source 3. Their partial acceptance preserves the assigned environmental preference. In the caf\'e, a pair with zero earlier exchanges becomes the most frequent final-phase partnership, with 25 messages. Its members develop coordination proposals while disputing their implementation. These results show that partial acceptance can coexist with low source trust, and sustained coordination with continuing disagreement. AI paper

docs.title: ScoringBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Tabular Foundation Models with Proper Scoring Rules
docs.text:
ScoringBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Tabular Foundation Models with Proper Scoring Rules ScoringBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Tabular Foundation Models with Proper Scoring Rules arXiv:2603.29928v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN, TabICL, ExaOneTabular, and Nori already produce full predictive distributions, yet prevailing regression benchmarks evaluate them almost exclusively via point-estimate metrics such as RMSE. This overlooks the distributional information these models are designed to provide. We introduce ScoringBench, an open and extensible benchmark that evaluates tabular regression models under a comprehensive suite of proper scoring rules - including (weighted) CRPS, energy scores and interval scores - alongside standard point metrics. ScoringBench covers 101 regression datasets from diverse domains, supports transparent community contributions via a git-based leaderboard, and provides two complementary ranking protocols: an ordinal Demsar/autorank approach and a magnitude-preserving $z$-score ranking approach. Our evaluation of various model types, including (fine-tuned) tabular foundation models, gradient-boosted trees, and MLPs, shows that model rankings shift depending on the chosen scoring rule. Models that perform well on point-estimate metrics can rank lower on probabilistic ones. These findings demonstrate that evaluation metric selection is a core modeling decision and a domain-specific requirement for applications where certain types of errors carry higher consequences. AI paper

docs.title: Logarithmic Scores, Power-Law Discoveries: Disentangling Measurement from Coverage in Agent-Based Evaluation
docs.text:
Logarithmic Scores, Power-Law Discoveries: Disentangling Measurement from Coverage in Agent-Based Evaluation Logarithmic Scores, Power-Law Discoveries: Disentangling Measurement from Coverage in Agent-Based Evaluation arXiv:2604.00477v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM-based agent judges are an emerging approach to evaluating conversational AI, yet a fundamental uncertainty remains: can we trust their assessments, and if so, how many are needed? Through 960 sessions with two model pairs across 15 tasks, we show that persona-based agent judges produce evaluations indistinguishable from human raters in a Turing-style validation. We then identify a score-coverage dissociation: quality scores improve logarithmically with panel size, while unique issue discoveries follow a sublinear power law-both exhibit diminishing returns, but scores saturate roughly twice as fast as discoveries. We hypothesize this reflects a power law distribution of the finding space: critical issues are discovered first by small panels, while corner cases require progressively larger panels, analogous to species accumulation curves in ecology. The mechanism traces to ensemble diversity-Big Five personality conditioning makes agents probe different quality dimensions, with expert judges acting as adversarial probes that push discovery into the tail of the finding distribution. A controlled ablation confirms that structured persona conditioning, not simple prompting, is required to produce these scaling properties. AI paper

docs.title: Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability
docs.text:
Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability arXiv:2604.01151v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems, they introduce risks of covert coordination that may evade standard forms of human oversight. While linear probes on model activations have shown promise for detecting deception in single-agent settings, collusion is inherently a multi-agent phenomenon, and the use of internal representations for detecting collusion between agents remains unexplored. We introduce NARCBench, a benchmark for evaluating collusion detection under environment distribution shift, and propose five probing techniques that aggregate per-agent deception scores to classify scenarios at the group level, evaluated across four open-weight models (Qwen3-32B, Llama-3.1-70B, DeepSeek-R1 32B, GPT-OSS-20B) and six probe architectures. We frame this as a distributed anomaly detection problem, identifying three collusion signatures that map onto distinct anomaly types and detection paradigms. Every model reaches 1.00 AUROC in-distribution; on our strongest model (Llama-3.1-70B), our five probing techniques achieve 0.73 to 0.93 AUROC when transferred zero-shot to structurally different multi-agent scenarios and 0.99 to 1.00 on a steganographic blackjack card-counting task, with detection performance scaling with model capability. We find that no single probing technique dominates across all collusion types, consistent with the framework's prediction that different anomaly types require different detection paradigms. This work takes a step toward multi-agent interpretability: extending white-box inspection from single models to multi-agent contexts, where detection requires aggregating signals across agents. These results suggest that model internals provide a complementary signal to text-level monitoring for detecting multi-agent collusion. Code and data available at https://github.com/aaronrose227/narcbench. AI paper

docs.title: Mitigating Distribution Sharpening in Math RLVR via Distribution-Aligned Hint Synthesis and Backward Hint Annealing
docs.text:
Mitigating Distribution Sharpening in Math RLVR via Distribution-Aligned Hint Synthesis and Backward Hint Annealing Mitigating Distribution Sharpening in Math RLVR via Distribution-Aligned Hint Synthesis and Backward Hint Annealing arXiv:2604.07747v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), challenging math questions whose sampled groups remain uniformly incorrect yield no informative update, letting easier questions dominate actor updates. This imbalance can contribute to distribution sharpening: low-$k$ accuracy improves while problem coverage contracts. Hint scaffolding can restore informative updates by revealing a prefix of a verified teacher solution. However, existing hint-based approaches still face two issues: teacher--student distribution mismatch and the need to reduce hint exposure to match no-hint evaluation. We address these issues through two components. Distribution-Aligned Hint Synthesis (DAHS) constructs verified teacher hints conditioned on student-style responses. Backward Hint Annealing (BHA) anneals hint exposure across length buckets as bucket accuracy improves. BHA also uses per-question hint dropout to keep no-hint rollouts throughout RL training. Under the DAPO training framework, our method improves both pass@1 and pass@2048 over DAPO on AIME24/25/26 for Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base, and improves pass@1 on five secondary math benchmarks (Olympiad, MATH500, Minerva Math, AMC23, and GSM8K). On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, the gains concentrate in the high-$k$ regime without recovering the base model's coverage. Overall, when verified teacher prefixes are available, DAHS+BHA mitigates DAPO-induced contraction of high-$k$ problem coverage in the evaluated challenging-math RLVR settings. AI paper

docs.title: Agentic Architect: An Agentic AI Framework for Architecture Design Exploration and Optimization
docs.text:
Agentic Architect: An Agentic AI Framework for Architecture Design Exploration and Optimization Agentic Architect: An Agentic AI Framework for Architecture Design Exploration and Optimization arXiv:2604.25083v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Computer Architecture research has traditionally required the exploration of vast, highly complex design spaces through manual human effort. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to accelerate this process by enabling fast and automated implementation and testing of different architectural mechanisms and their combinations. We introduce Agentic Architect, a framework for agentic CPU microarchitectural design-space exploration and optimization. The Agentic Architect combines LLM-driven code evolution with cycle-accurate simulation and hardware cost modeling to explore performance, area, and power tradeoffs. Starting from a seed design, the LLM is prompted to explore the design space by implementing changes, guided by prior evaluation feedback. Each new design is compiled, simulated on training workloads, evaluated against the optimization objective, and constrained by area and power budgets. Its score and diagnostics update the candidate population and guide subsequent iterations.
  We evaluate the Agentic Architect framework across prefetching, cache replacement, and branch prediction. On 213 traces spanning five benchmark suites, its evolved prefetchers lead the evaluated L1D and L2 designs, delivering up to 6.7% and 2.6% additional speedup, respectively, over the strongest state-of-the-art design, while the best evolved cache replacement design improves over Mockingjay by up to 1.7%. Moreover, across 191 branch-prediction traces, the evolved branch predictor achieves 97.62% of TAGE-SC-L's geometric mean IPC at 10.58% of its area. Our analysis highlights the importance of seed selection, hardware constraints, and training workloads in shaping search outcomes. Overall, Agentic Architect establishes the first end-to-end framework for agentic CPU microarchitectural design optimization, opening a new direction for architecture research. AI paper

docs.title: OracleProto: A Reproducible Framework for Benchmarking LLM Forecasting via Knowledge Cutoffs and Temporal Masking
docs.text:
OracleProto: A Reproducible Framework for Benchmarking LLM Forecasting via Knowledge Cutoffs and Temporal Masking OracleProto: A Reproducible Framework for Benchmarking LLM Forecasting via Knowledge Cutoffs and Temporal Masking arXiv:2605.03762v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Forecasting is a composite capability encompassing information gathering, evidence integration, situational assessment, and decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) combine reasoning and tool use, offering new avenues for automated forecasting and decision support. Yet LLM forecasting evaluation faces a structural challenge: live benchmarks support prospective assessment, but limited question reuse and changing information conditions make results difficult to reproduce and compare; retrospective benchmarks offer reproducibility but risk information leakage. We introduce OracleProto, a reproducible framework for evaluating LLM forecasting in a controlled, temporally masked environment. Through model knowledge cutoff constraints and temporal masking, OracleProto constructs a temporal sandbox for real-world web retrieval, audits information boundaries through leakage detection, and reconstructs resolved events as forecasting instances. Discrete answer normalization and hierarchical scoring enable unified evaluation. We evaluate 27 model-configuration pairs on 300 FutureX-Past-derived questions over 24,300 prediction trials, assessing forecasting quality, sampling stability, and cost efficiency under controlled information boundaries. An audit finds only 1.37% residual leakage in retrieval results after temporal masking and leakage filtering. OracleProto retains resolved forecasting tasks as reusable evaluation resources under explicit temporal boundaries, supporting continual accumulation of forecasting datasets and systematic evaluation of forecasting capabilities. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OracleProto-2E3A/. AI paper

docs.title: VibeServe: Can AI Agents Build Bespoke LLM Serving Systems?
docs.text:
VibeServe: Can AI Agents Build Bespoke LLM Serving Systems? VibeServe: Can AI Agents Build Bespoke LLM Serving Systems? arXiv:2605.06068v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: For years, we have built LLM serving systems like any other critical infrastructure, with a single general-purpose stack hand-tuned over many engineer-years to support every model and workload. In this paper, we take the opposite bet and let coding agents automatically synthesize bespoke serving systems for different usage scenarios. We propose VibeServe, the first agentic loop that generates entire LLM serving stacks end-to-end. VibeServe uses an outer loop to plan and track the search over system designs, and an inner loop to implement candidates, check correctness, and measure performance on the target benchmark. In standard serving settings, VibeServe matches vLLM and SGLang on Llama-3.1-8B, and delivers 2.3x the goodput of a tuned SGLang for a 397B MoE model on four AMD MI300As. In five non-standard scenarios, VibeServe outperforms existing systems by exploiting opportunities that generic systems miss, spanning non-standard model architectures, workload knowledge, and hardware-specific optimizations. Together, these results argue that infrastructure software should favor generation-time specialization over runtime generality. Code is available at https://github.com/uw-syfi/vibesys. AI paper

docs.title: Tools as Continuous Flow for Evolving Agentic Reasoning
docs.text:
Tools as Continuous Flow for Evolving Agentic Reasoning Tools as Continuous Flow for Evolving Agentic Reasoning arXiv:2605.07339v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in orchestrating tools for reasoning tasks. However, existing methods rely on a step-wise paradigm that lacks a global perspective, which causes error accumulation over long horizons and restricts generalization to unseen tools. To overcome these limitations, we propose Tools as Continuous Flow for Evolving Agentic Reasoning (FlowAgent), which reconceptualizes tool chaining as continuous trajectory generation within a semantic space. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we introduce the first plan-level closed-loop benchmark dedicated to plan-level agentic reasoning in dynamic real-world environments. Specifically, the proposed FlowAgent leverages conditional flow matching to generate continuous latent trajectories, providing a global planning perspective to ensure coherent and robust tool execution. Theoretically, we establish formal bounds on utility convergence and prove that our continuous formulation fundamentally guarantees robust generalization and error attenuation. Empirical evaluations show that FlowAgent achieves superior robustness and adaptability in long-horizon reasoning tasks. AI paper

docs.title: MemQ: Integrating Q-Learning into Self-Evolving Memory Agents over Provenance DAGs
docs.text:
MemQ: Integrating Q-Learning into Self-Evolving Memory Agents over Provenance DAGs MemQ: Integrating Q-Learning into Self-Evolving Memory Agents over Provenance DAGs arXiv:2605.08374v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Episodic memory allows LLM agents to accumulate and retrieve experience, but current methods treat each memory independently, i.e., evaluating retrieval quality in isolation without accounting for the dependency chains through which memories enable the creation of future memories. We introduce MemQ, which applies TD($\lambda$) eligibility traces to memory Q-values, propagating credit backward through a provenance DAG that records which memories were retrieved when each new memory was created. Credit weight decays as $(\gamma\lambda)^d$ with DAG depth $d$, replacing temporal distance with structural proximity. We formalize this setting as an Exogenous-Context MDP, separating externally supplied tasks from the evolving memory store, and represent retrieval-set values by a first-order mean of per-memory values plus an explicit approximation residual. Across five interaction, code-generation, and agentic benchmarks, MemQ improves average held-out, final runtime, and cumulative success rates over the baseline with the highest average for each metric by 2.53, 4.23, and 2.13 percentage points, respectively. Ablations on LiveCodeBench, BFCL, and DSBench support the benefit of bootstrapping and multi-depth credit propagation. Analyses of Q-values and runtime learning show that learned memory values are associated with subsequent success and that MemQ retains more of its historical task coverage. We also explore the limits of MemQ's benefits using multiple-choice reasoning tasks, where limited interaction offers fewer opportunities to reuse procedural experience. Code is available at https://github.com/jwliao-ai/MemQ. AI paper

docs.title: RewardHarness: Self-Evolving Agentic Post-Training
docs.text:
RewardHarness: Self-Evolving Agentic Post-Training RewardHarness: Self-Evolving Agentic Post-Training arXiv:2605.08703v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Aligning generative models with human preferences remains a central challenge. While RLHF is widely adopted, it relies on large-scale preference data. This limitation is particularly evident in evaluating instruction-guided image edits, even though humans can often learn such preferences from only a few examples. We present RewardHarness, a training-free, self-evolving agentic reward framework that reframes reward modeling as context evolution rather than weight optimization. Instead of learning from large-scale annotations, RewardHarness aligns with human preferences by iteratively evolving a library of tools and skills from as few as 100 preference demonstrations. Given a source image, an edited image, and an editing instruction, an orchestrator agent selects the most relevant subset of tools and skills from the maintained library, and sub-agents invoke them to construct a reasoning chain that produces a reward score. By comparing predicted scores with ground-truth preferences and analyzing successes and failures in the reasoning process, the orchestrator automatically refines its library of tools and skills without additional human annotation. Using only 0.05% of the EditReward preference data, RewardHarness achieves 47.4% average accuracy on EditReward-Bench K=2/3/4 and GenAI-Bench, surpassing GPT-5 by 5.3 points. When used as a reward signal in FlowGRPO, RL-tuned models achieve 3.52 on ImgEdit-Bench. Code and model are available at the project page: https://rewardharness.com/ AI paper

docs.title: Data-driven Circuit Discovery for Interpretability of Language Models
docs.text:
Data-driven Circuit Discovery for Interpretability of Language Models Data-driven Circuit Discovery for Interpretability of Language Models arXiv:2605.09129v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Circuit study aims to explain how language models (LMs) implement a task by localizing and interpreting a circuit: a computational subgraph responsible for a specific model's behavior. Existing methods for circuit localization are largely hypothesis-driven: they define a task through a dataset, assume that all examples in the task are implemented by the same mechanism, and apply circuit discovery to obtain a single circuit. This workflow does not account for mechanistic diversity within a task, where different examples may rely on different mechanisms. We first show that when a dataset mixes tasks processed through distinct mechanisms, current circuit discovery can combine these mechanisms into a single circuit while retaining faithfulness comparable to circuits discovered on each task separately. Across four tasks and three models, we further provide evidence for such mechanistic diversity within individual tasks. To account for this diversity, we propose Data-driven Circuit Discovery (DCD), which modifies the circuit-discovery workflow by adding a grouping step before the discovery. The grouping step aims to partition the dataset into subsets of examples that rely on similar mechanisms. We instantiate this step with clustering over per-example attribution patterns (DCD-Cluster). Across four tasks and three models, DCD-Cluster decomposes the dataset into multiple subsets whose circuits exhibit distinct faithfulness patterns, providing useful hypotheses about mechanistic differences among examples. AI paper

docs.title: Verifiable Process Rewards for Agentic Reasoning
docs.text:
Verifiable Process Rewards for Agentic Reasoning Verifiable Process Rewards for Agentic Reasoning arXiv:2605.10325v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) has improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet existing approaches predominantly rely on sparse outcome-level feedback, posing a substantial credit-assignment challenge in long-horizon agentic tasks. In this work, we study structured agentic reasoning problems that admit symbolic or algorithmic task-solving oracles. We propose Verifiable Process Rewards (VPR), a training framework that repurposes such task oracles as action-level process verifiers, providing dense rewards for intermediate actions and enabling fine-grained credit assignment. We instantiate VPR in three distinct settings: a search-based oracle for Sokoban, a constraint-based oracle for Sudoku, and a posterior-based oracle for Minesweeper. To optimize policies with these rewards, we introduce oracle-guided state-group rollout and locally normalized optimization. Empirically, VPR-trained Qwen3-4B outperforms outcome-reward GRPO and VinePPO across all three training environments. When jointly trained on math data and all three game environments, VPR achieves the highest average general-reasoning performance and strongest agentic results among the compared training configurations. To further assess its applicability to more general agentic tool-use settings, we apply VPR-style action-level supervision to $\tau^2$-bench using an expert LLM as a reference policy and observe improved performance over outcome-reward GRPO on held-out tasks. Together, these results position VPR as a promising approach for leveraging reliable task oracles to improve agentic reasoning, while highlighting its dependence on the availability and reliability of task oracles and the challenge of extending intermediate verification to less structured, open-ended environments. AI paper

docs.title: Argumentation-Based Person-Tailored Storytelling for Older Adults: A Reflective Hybrid AI Architecture
docs.text:
Argumentation-Based Person-Tailored Storytelling for Older Adults: A Reflective Hybrid AI Architecture Argumentation-Based Person-Tailored Storytelling for Older Adults: A Reflective Hybrid AI Architecture arXiv:2605.10531v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: This work investigates knowledge-driven, large language model (LLM)-based storytelling for older adults. We present a reflective storytelling agent integrating knowledge graphs, user modelling, and argumentation theory to guide person-tailored narratives. Argument mining supports inspection of argument structure, while persona grounding is assessed separately against structured information.
  The study comprised three phases. Phase I involved 11 domain experts whose feedback informed system refinement. Phase II involved 55 older adults evaluating narratives based on predefined personas across inquiry, deliberation, and persuasion purposes and two creativity levels. Phase III compared the full system with an argumentation-scheme ablation and standard LLM baseline, and validated zero-shot argument mining against human-consensus annotations.
  In Phase II, the intended purpose was recognised in 30.6% of 330 assessments; 33.3% indicated no clear purpose and 36.1% another purpose. Cultural relatability was descriptively associated with future-use intention, although 30 of 55 participants did not intend to use similar functionality.
  In Phase III, 67.6% of applicable sampled statements were persona-grounded in the full system versus 57.9% without scheme guidance, a non-significant difference. Scheme guidance increased explicit premises without changing claim counts. The full system showed substantially greater sampled grounding than the standard LLM baseline. Zero-shot argument mining showed moderate agreement with human-consensus annotations, supporting its role as an inspection aid rather than a verifier. These findings highlight the potential and limitations of reflective, person-tailored LLM storytelling for older adults. AI paper

docs.title: Energy per Successful Goal: Goal-Level Energy Accounting for Agentic AI Systems
docs.text:
Energy per Successful Goal: Goal-Level Energy Accounting for Agentic AI Systems Energy per Successful Goal: Goal-Level Energy Accounting for Agentic AI Systems arXiv:2605.22883v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Current AI energy benchmarks measure consumption per model invocation. For agentic systems, where a single user goal may trigger multistep orchestration, tool calls, retries, and failure recovery, the invocation count is an implementation artifact rather than a task property, and per inference normalization misrepresents the energy cost of completing a goal. We present A-LEMS (Agentic LLM Energy Measurement System), a cross layer framework that redefines the unit of AI energy accounting as Energy per Successful Goal (EpG): total workflow energy across all attempts, including failures and retries, divided by successfully completed goals. A-LEMS combines a temporal boundary model, a five layer attribution pipeline mapping hardware signals (RAPL on x86; SPBM and DCGM on ARM) to workflow energy, and a reproducibility protocol binding every measurement to hardware, environment, and runtime configuration. Building on EpG, we define the Orchestration Overhead Index (OOI), the ratio of agentic to linear EpG on matched goals under identical success criteria. Across nine task families on Intel x86 and NVIDIA Grace GB10 ARM, CPU only OOI ranges 0.35x to 11.07x. Including GPU dynamic energy, which accounts for 83.8% of agentic EpG in local inference, widens this to 0.4x to 26.48x, so CPU only measurement understates overhead about twofold for reasoning tasks. For remote inference, network wait energy shifts OOI from 2.5x to 2.35x. The overhead arises from orchestration structure (planning, retries, recovery) that induces additional inference calls, not from costlier individual calls. The metric is not biased upward: single tool calculator dispatch inverts to OOI = 0.61x (95% CI [0.35, 0.97]) on x86.
